complaint: A 75-year-old man visited a physician for abdominal pain and vomiting.

events.t: A 75-year-old man visited a physician for abdominal pain and vomiting.
Abdominal computed tomography (CT) indicated a ruptured pancreaticoduodenal aneurysm and stenosis of the root of the CA.
He was transferred to our hospital.
He had a past medical history of mental retardation and gastric cancer that had been treated with a distal gastrectomy with Billroth-I reconstruction.
Blood examination findings revealed an elevation of inflammation markers (white blood cell 19,010/μL, C-reactive protein 7.08 mg/dL) and anemia (hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL).

Emergency angiography revealed stenosis of the root of the CA, and spindle-shaped dilatation and pseudoaneurysm formation were observed both in the posterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery (PIPDA) and in the anterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery (AIPDA).
Contrast medium extravasation from the PIPDA was observed.
Coil embolization was performed on the PIPDA to the posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal artery, which was the bleeding source.
At that time, coil embolization of the AIPDA was not performed because no extravasation of the contrast agent was observed.
After coil embolization of the PIPDA, the celiac arterial region was visualized from the anterior inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery via the gastroduodenal artery.
Then, the patient was hospitalized for follow-up, but right-sided flank pain appeared on the sixth day after the embolization.
CT showed a swollen gallbladder and encapsulated fluid retention around it.
It suggested that the wall was broken at the fundus of the gallbladder.
An emergency laparotomy was then performed because gallbladder necrosis was suspected due to the decreased blood flow in the CA region.
The wall of the gallbladder was found to be partially necrotic.
The gallbladder was distended, and bile leakage was not observed.
In addition, the MAL was dissected to improve blood flow in the CA region.
A fibrous ligament anterior to the CA was confirmed, and the MAL was transected to expose the wall of the CA and the aorta.
The blood flow in the celiac and hepatic arteries was confirmed by echography, and the surgery was completed after the abdominal cavity was thoroughly washed.
After the operation, the patient entered the emergency care unit under intubation.
Extubation was performed on postoperative day (POD) 2.
Perioperative blood pressure was controlled with antihypertensive agent so that systolic blood pressure was around 100 mmHg.
Pleural effusion and ascites were observed, and bilateral thoracic drainage and ascites drainage were performed on POD 4.
The abdominal CT scan on POD 4 determined that the stenosis of the CA was released and that the size of the untreated aneurysm of the AIPDA was unchanged.
However, the patient exhaled blood on the evening of POD 8, and an emergency CT scan and upper gastrointestinal endoscopy were performed.
At that time, no obvious source of bleeding was found, and fresh blood had accumulated in the esophagus.
The emergency CT findings showed little change in the peritoneal hematoma and extravasations from the untreated AIPDA aneurysm.
In addition, the AIPDA aneurysm, which had been unchanged in the previous CT scan, increased slightly from the previous CT scan.
The patient soon exhaled blood again, and his systolic blood pressure dropped rapidly to less than 60 mmHg.
Because of heavy bleeding, endotracheal intubation was performed to control the airway.
After transfusion, another upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was performed.
Persistent bleeding from the posterior wall of the descending duodenum was observed, and the duodenal wall broke down.
We consulted radiology about the indication of endovascular treatment, but it was judged difficult because of vital instability.
The patient died of hemorrhagic shock 12 h after the first hematemesis.
An autopsy was not performed because the consent of the family was not obtained.
Eventually, the rupture of an untreated AIPDA aneurysm was diagnosed as the cause of death.

pearls: In the present case, CA stenosis due to MALS was considered to be the cause of the pancreaticoduodenal aneurysm.
Although 3D-CT was not used in the present case, the stenosis was considered type B, and the MAL division was recommended.

src.title: Metachronous rupture of a residual pancreaticoduodenal aneurysm after release of the median arcuate ligament: a case report
src.authors: Nana Kimura, Koshi Matsui, Kazuto Shibuya et al.

complaint: A 31-year-old male with a body mass index of 28 kg/m² presented with a six-month history of right anterior knee pain associated with mechanical locking and catching following an injury during a soccer game.

events.t: A 31-year-old male with a body mass index of 28 kg/m² presented with a six-month history of right anterior knee pain associated with mechanical locking and catching following an injury during a soccer game.
Symptoms persisted despite a course of nonoperative management that included physical therapy, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medication, and activity modification.

The available source documentation did not provide sufficient detail to reliably report the duration of each individual conservative modality, prior knee trauma, activity level, or additional relevant medical and surgical history; these details were, therefore, not retrospectively inferred.
Clinical examination demonstrated tenderness over the anterior knee, a positive McMurray test, and limited range of motion from 10° to 110°.

The available preoperative documentation did not reliably report effusion, joint-line tenderness, patellofemoral provocative signs, ligamentous testing, or the presence or absence of a palpable mass; these findings were therefore not reconstructed retrospectively.

Preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the right knee was performed without intravenous contrast using coronal proton-density (PD), coronal fat-suppressed T2, sagittal proton-density, sagittal fat-suppressed T2, axial fat-suppressed PD, and sagittal T2 anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) sequences.

MRI demonstrated a flattened hypointense triangular lesion measuring approximately 1.4 × 0.5 × 0.2 cm located anterior to the anterior cruciate ligament, contiguous with adjacent scarring of Hoffa's fat pad.
The lesion was associated with trace knee effusion and lateral meniscal abnormalities.
Although MRI suggested a fat-containing lesion arising near the infrapatellar fat pad, the precise tissue origin could not be established preoperatively.
Following discussion of the risks, benefits, and alternatives, the patient provided informed consent for right knee arthroscopy.
Written informed consent was also obtained for publication of this case report and the accompanying images.
After informed consent was obtained, the patient was correctly identified in the preoperative holding area, and the operative knee was marked with the surgeon's initials to confirm laterality.
The patient was transported to the operating room and positioned supine.
General anesthesia was induced, a formal surgical time-out was performed, and prophylactic intravenous antibiotics were administered.
The right lower extremity was prepared and draped in the standard sterile fashion with the thigh secured in an arthroscopic leg holder, and a thigh tourniquet was used.
A standard anterolateral viewing portal was established using a #11 blade, and a 30° Stryker arthroscope (Stryker, Kalamazoo, MI, USA) was introduced into the knee joint.
Under direct visualization, an anteromedial working portal was established using spinal-needle localization.
A systematic diagnostic arthroscopy was then performed with sequential evaluation of the suprapatellar pouch, patellofemoral joint, medial compartment, lateral compartment, and intercondylar notch.
A loose body measuring greater than 5 mm was identified within the patellofemoral compartment and removed using suction and arthroscopic forceps.
The lesion demonstrated a fibrofatty gross appearance and was described intraoperatively as a remnant of Hoffa's fat pad.

Histopathologic examination was not obtained, and the operative report did not document a discrete donor site or direct continuity between the loose body and the infrapatellar fat pad; therefore, its tissue of origin remains presumed.
A prominent traumatic erythematous plica was also identified and resected using a motorized shaver and arthroscopic wand.
Inflamed, hypertrophic-appearing synovial tissue was resected from the medial, lateral, and patellofemoral compartments with minimal bleeding.
A lateral meniscal tear was treated with partial lateral meniscectomy using hand instruments and a 3.5-mm motorized shaver, with the remaining meniscus debrided to a smooth, stable border.
The operative report did not further specify the tear morphology or subregion.
It also noted an injured chondral area whose edges were probed for stability but did not provide a formal cartilage grade or precise location.
Local anesthetic consisting of equal parts 0.5% bupivacaine and 2% lidocaine was injected at the arthroscopic portal sites.
The knee was irrigated, the portals were closed with 3-0 nylon sutures, and a sterile dressing was applied.
The patient tolerated the procedure without intraoperative complication and was transferred to the recovery area in stable condition.
Postoperative management included weight-bearing as tolerated, anti-embolic stockings, and aspirin 325 mg daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis.
Rehabilitation included straight-leg raises, quadriceps-setting exercises, prone hangs, and active-assisted knee flexion initiated in the recovery room.
At the six-week follow-up, the patient demonstrated marked short-term improvement following combined arthroscopic treatment.
The Visual Analog Scale pain score decreased from 7/10 to 1/10, mechanical locking resolved, and range of motion improved from 10°-110° preoperatively to 0°-130°.
No complication was reported at this visit.

A validated knee-specific patient-reported outcome measure and longer-term follow-up were not available in the source materials used for this revision; therefore, no claims regarding recurrence or long-term efficacy are made.

pearls: The differential diagnosis of an intra-articular loose body or mass in this location includes an osteochondral fragment, meniscal fragment, synovial chondromatosis, para-articular chondroma, lipoma arborescens or another lipomatous lesion, and tenosynovial giant-cell tumor.
MRI remains the primary imaging modality for characterizing Hoffa's fat-pad pathology and narrowing the differential diagnosis.
Arthroscopy therefore served as an important complementary diagnostic and therapeutic modality.

These limitations reduce diagnostic certainty but do not diminish the educational value of recognizing an unusual fibrofatty intra-articular lesion and considering an appropriately broad differential diagnosis.
MRI and arthroscopy should therefore be viewed as complementary rather than interchangeable diagnostic tools.

src.title: Arthroscopic Management of an Unusual Fibrofatty Loose Body Presumed to Arise From Hoffa’s Fat Pad: A Case Report
src.authors: John A Spallanzani, Henry K Mah, Jamil Ayinla et al.

complaint: A 55-year-old lady complained of left shoulder pain.

events.t: A 55-year-old lady complained of left shoulder pain.
She worked as a clerical officer, and found it difficult to do any heavy lifting, overhead work or to sleep at night.
The pain started gradually over the last 10 months, she did not recall any trauma or injuries.
She had no significant weight loss or constitutional symptoms, there were no red flags and her history was otherwise normal.
On physical exam, she had painful impingement of her left shoulder with some weakness of her rotator cuff muscles.
Neer and Hawkins signs were both positive.
She had no lymphadenopathy and there was no evidence of any skin changes.
Blood investigations were normal and plain films of the left shoulder were unremarkable.
She had temporal relief from a steroid injection and physiotherapy.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the patient’s right shoulder showed supraspinatus tendinopathy with a partial tear.
There was a soft tissue mass in the subacromial space measuring 2.5 × 1.0 × 0.5 cm.
There were no features of an aggressive lesion or any local infiltration.
Following a discussion of the risks and benefits of conservative versus surgical intervention, she decided to undergo an arthroscopic excision biopsy.
At surgery her glenohumeral joint was normal.
The subacromial space revealed a soft tissue mass.
It was attached to the bursal tissue without any obvious connection to muscle.
The mass was excised by marginal excision and subacromial bursectomy was completed.
The gross specimen measured 2.3 × 1.0 × 0.5 cm.
Specimens were taken with arthroscopic biopsy forceps and the mass was removed en bloc by use of a synovator.
Histology showed a lipomatous lesion with a surface synovial lining and a focus of lymphoplasmacytic infiltration.
At 5 years follow up, the patient had a full active range of movement of her shoulder and normal power of her rotator cuff.

pearls: Tumours in the shoulder region such as metastatic carcinoma and myeloma should not be overlooked, as they are not uncommon and can be misdiagnosed as rotator cuff tears.
A systemic approach for abnormal causes of SIS is recommended to avoid misdiagnosing rare or sinister pathologies, which may hinder recovery and/or lead to poor results.

src.title: Subacromial impingement by a lipoma arborescens
src.authors: Mohamed Elamin, Venkatramana Yeluri, Hisham Khatir et al.

complaint: A 42-year-old averagely built male without known comorbidities presented with pain in the right heel lasting for one year and swelling for six months.

events.t: A 42-year-old averagely built male without known comorbidities presented with pain in the right heel lasting for one year and swelling for six months.
There was no history of specific trauma associated with the onset of symptoms.
Initially, the pain occurred only during running and was relieved with rest.
However, the pain intensity gradually increased over the following five months.
The heel swelling developed insidiously and worsened as the pain intensified.
Over the past month, the pain occurred even at rest and was relieved only by over-the-counter pain-relieving medications, which he required on most days of the week.
There was no history of significant weight loss, reduced appetite, or a family history of skeletal tumors.
A regional examination revealed a heterogeneous, tender swelling over the right heel.
The overlying skin appeared normal, with no erythema or venous prominence.
Tenderness was noted over the lateral and plantar surfaces of the right heel, and the calcaneal squeeze test elicited moderate to severe pain.
The ankle’s range of motion was full and painless, with no signs of neurovascular compromise.
The American Orthopaedic Foot & Ankle Society (AOFAS) ankle-hindfoot score was 55 out of a maximum score of 100.
Laboratory investigations revealed no significant abnormalities.
Standard radiographs showed a cystic lesion involving nearly the entire calcaneus, with thinning of the cortex and a cortical breach on the undersurface, but no cortical expansion.
MRI demonstrated a lobulated margin area with altered signal intensity, appearing mildly hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images.
The lesion measured 51 mm in the anteroposterior plane, 31 mm in the mediolateral plane, and 39 mm in the supero-inferior plane.
It was associated with thinning of the calcaneal cortex, with cortical breach in some areas.
A PET-CT scan revealed no evidence of a primary tumor elsewhere or metastasis.
The patient was initially placed in a temporary back slab to prevent further progression of a pathological fracture and was allowed to mobilize with crutches.
A core needle biopsy of the lesion was performed, revealing a few multinucleated giant cells without evidence of mitosis or necrosis.
Treatment options were discussed with the patient, and written informed consent was obtained for lesion excision followed by bone grafting.

Given the anticipated large post-curettage calcaneal defect and the high cost and unavailability of allografts due to the lack of a bone bank, we opted to use autologous non-vascularized fibular strut grafts.
This approach also helped avoid potential complications associated with the use of bone cement.
Under spinal anesthesia, an autologous tricortical bone graft was harvested from the ipsilateral iliac crest, while fibular strut grafts were obtained from the ipsilateral fibula.
The calcaneus was accessed via a lateral approach, and a cortical window was created to expose the tumor.
The tumor tissue was meticulously scraped out until healthy, bleeding bone was observed.
A phenol solution was applied to eliminate residual tumor cells, followed by thorough drainage and rinsing with water.

The fibular strut grafts were then inserted into the calcaneal cavity, and the remaining cavity was packed with tricortical iliac crest graft pieces and artificial bone graft in the form of synthetic hydroxyapatite granules.
Finally, the cortical window was repositioned like a trap door.
Histopathological examination demonstrated fascicles of spindle cells with elongated vesicular nuclei and moderate cytoplasm, interspersed with multinucleated giant cells.
No evidence of mitosis or necrosis was observed.
The diagnosis was confirmed as BFH of the calcaneus.
The leg was placed in a below-knee plaster slab, and intermittent ankle mobilization, as tolerated by the patient, was initiated from the first postoperative day.
The immediate postoperative radiograph showed no evidence of residual lytic lesions.
Right lower limb toe-touch weight-bearing mobilization with crutch support began on the second postoperative day.
Stitches were removed two weeks post-surgery, and partial weight-bearing was permitted six weeks after the procedure.
Full weight-bearing was allowed after three months.
At the five-year follow-up, the patient was doing well without any symptoms, achieving an AOFAS ankle-hindfoot score of 100.
He demonstrated a full range of motion at the ankle, with adequate graft healing and no signs of local recurrence.

pearls: BFH of the calcaneus is an extremely rare tumor, making accurate diagnosis crucial.

src.title: Benign Fibrous Histiocytoma of the Calcaneus: A Case Report of a Rare Bone Tumor
src.authors: Abheek Kar, Soumyadip Sen, Abhishek Das et al.

complaint: A 21-year-old female patient presented with missing teeth in the anterior maxillary region following a road traffic accident, associated with substantial loss of the alveolar ridge.

events.t: A 21-year-old female patient presented with missing teeth in the anterior maxillary region following a road traffic accident, associated with substantial loss of the alveolar ridge.

Clinical examination revealed a localized deficiency of the anterior maxillary ridge with reduced buccolingual dimensions and loss of the facial cortical plate, resulting in bone dehiscence at the proposed implant sites.
The surrounding soft tissues were clinically healthy, with no signs of active infection or inflammation.
The adjacent teeth and periodontal tissues were evaluated to determine the suitability of the planned implant sites.
Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) was performed to assess the three-dimensional morphology and extent of the osseous defect.

Radiographic examination demonstrated inadequate bone volume for predictable conventional implant placement, particularly in the facial aspect of the anterior maxilla, with evidence of bone dehiscence.
The bone density at the proposed implant region was classified as D3, with a mean radiographic density of approximately 427 HU.

This relatively low-density bone indicated a compromised bony substrate and was considered during treatment planning because reduced bone density may influence primary implant stability and the regenerative requirements of the site.
However, HU values obtained from CBCT should be interpreted in relation to the imaging system and acquisition parameters rather than as an absolute measure of bone quality.
Based on the clinical and radiographic findings, the site was diagnosed as a post-traumatic anterior maxillary ridge deficiency with inadequate bone volume for ideal implant positioning.
Guided bone regeneration (GBR), a regenerative technique in which a barrier membrane is used to maintain a protected space for bone formation, was planned simultaneously with implant placement.

FDBA was selected as the grafting material to provide a scaffold within the deficient area, while an amnion-chorion membrane was used as a barrier to stabilize the graft and support compartmentalized tissue regeneration.

The treatment objective was to achieve adequate peri-implant hard-tissue volume while maintaining the three-dimensional ridge contour required for subsequent prosthetic rehabilitation and esthetic restoration.
Under local anaesthesia, a crestal incision was placed, and a full-thickness mucoperiosteal flap was reflected, followed by osteotomy preparation.
Two implants, each measuring 3.3 mm in diameter and 11.5 mm in length, were subsequently placed.
Primary stability was achieved, with an insertion torque of 37 Ncm.
To manage the dehiscence defect and augment the peri-implant bone volume, GBR was performed simultaneously with implant placement.
FDBA, obtained from the Tata Memorial Hospital Tissue Bank, Mumbai, was placed within the defect.

The grafted site was then covered with a resorbable placental amnion-chorion membrane (also procured from the Tata Memorial Hospital Tissue Bank, Mumbai) to provide a barrier against soft tissue infiltration and facilitate bone regeneration.
The surgical flap was repositioned and secured with interrupted sutures using 3-0 non-resorbable silk.
After a healing period of three months, the patient was recalled for phase II implant surgery.
Clinical and radiographic evaluation revealed satisfactory healing of the augmented ridge and stable implant placement.
Implant uncovering was performed under local anesthesia, followed by placement of appropriate healing abutments to facilitate peri-implant soft tissue conditioning.
The surgical site was managed uneventfully, and the patient was advised for follow-up and subsequent prosthetic rehabilitation.
At the time of reporting, the implants were clinically stable.
At the six-month follow-up, the surgical site demonstrated satisfactory healing with healthy peri-implant soft tissues and no clinical signs of inflammation or infection.
Radiographic evaluation revealed satisfactory bone formation around the implants with maintenance of the augmented bone volume.
The implants were clinically stable, indicating successful osseointegration.
Following confirmation of satisfactory healing and implant stability, the implants were exposed, and the prosthetic phase of treatment was initiated.
At the one-year post-prosthetic follow-up, the implants demonstrated satisfactory clinical and radiographic outcomes.
The peri-implant soft tissues appeared healthy and stable, with satisfactory maintenance of the gingival contour and aesthetics.
Radiographic evaluation revealed stable crestal bone levels with no significant peri-implant bone loss.
The prosthesis remained functionally stable, with no evidence of biological or mechanical complications, indicating successful maintenance of the augmented site and implant-supported rehabilitation.
Throughout the treatment and follow-up period, the patient reported no complications, such as infection or graft failure.
Clinical and radiographic evaluations confirmed stable peri-implant bone levels and healthy soft tissues.

This case emphasizes the importance of a combined approach involving initial implant placement along with bone grafting to manage significant bone deficiencies in the upper anterior teeth region, ensuring successful functional and aesthetic outcomes.

pearls: In this case, using FDBA was crucial for augmenting the deficient alveolar ridge, thereby creating a stable foundation for the dental implant.
Additionally, one important drawback of those non-resorbable membranes is the need for a second surgical procedure for their removal.
Therefore, the favorable healing observed in the present case should be interpreted as a clinical outcome of the combined regenerative protocol rather than attributed solely to the membrane.

src.title: Simultaneous Implant Placement and Guided Bone Regeneration Using Freeze-Dried Bone Allograft and Amnion–Chorion Membrane for Post-traumatic Anterior Maxillary Bone Dehiscence: A Case Report
src.authors: Aena J Pundir, Harsha P Tembhare, Siddharth Pundhir et al.

complaint: We were presented in the OPD with a seven-year-old male child complaining of pain and swelling around his right ankle joint while playing for three months.

events.t: We were presented in the OPD with a seven-year-old male child complaining of pain and swelling around his right ankle joint while playing for three months.
There was no history of trauma, fever, loss of weight or appetite.

On examination, there was diffuse hard swelling over the anterior ankle joint line with prominent lateral malleolus and restricted range of motion with no dorsiflexion beyond neutral, as shown in Figure 1, and plantar flexion up to 15 degrees, as shown in Figure 2.
Radiological investigation provided the following picture.
A lateral view and AP view X-ray of the preoperative ankle demonstrates a bony outgrowth from the talus directed posteriorly and laterally.
A CT scan revealed a bony tumor arising from the talar dome and extending into syndesmosis, as seen in Figure 4 and Figure 5, which are the coronal images, and Figure 6, which is the sagittal view.
MRI revealed the complete extent of the tumor with the cartilage cap and surrounding soft tissue compression, as seen in Figure 7 and Figure 8.
The posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament (PITFL) was found torn due to the pressure from the extensive tumor.
Operative technique
Under general anesthesia, the patient was positioned in a lateral position.
The tumor was dissected in both the anterolateral and posterolateral approaches.
This approach was chosen based on preoperative radiological imaging.
The extent and direction of the tumor were to be best approached by dual incisions, as mentioned above.

Soft tissue dissection was done in layers to approach the bony lesion, taking care to avoid damage to the sural nerve in the posterolateral approach and the intermediate branch of the superficial peroneal nerve in the anterolateral approach.
Complete excision of two tumors of size 13x 11 mm and 11x 6mm was done, and completeness was confirmed under C-arm imaging.
The excised tissue was sent for histopathological evaluation.
After the excision of the tumor, there was a gap between the tibia and the fibula on direct visualization.
When the ankle was checked for dorsiflexion and external rotation, there was further opening of the syndesmosis under intra-operative fluoroscopy in anteroposterior view.
Hence, it was diagnosed intraoperatively that the syndesmosis was unstable.
A decision was made to stabilize the syndesmosis with a 3.5 mm cortical screw, as seen in Figure 9.
The posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament was seen to be ruptured and was repaired anatomically with fiber wire no 2 for added syndesmotic stability.
Skin and subcutaneous tissue were closed in layers.
The postoperative period was relatively uneventful; edge necrosis of the posterolateral wound occurred, which completely healed by secondary intention in two weeks.
Histopathology was reported as cartilage-capped mature lamellar bone with enchondral ossification, which is consistent with osteochondroma.
No evidence of malignancy seen".
He was started on ankle range of motion exercises after two days of surgery and was not allowed to bear weight.
When not exercising, he was immobilized with a removable splint.
At three weeks, he was allowed to partially bear weight as tolerated.
When reviewed at six weeks, he had progressed to full weight bearing and was not experiencing any pain.
At six months follow-up, the range of motion had improved significantly to 30 degrees of plantar flexion, 5 degrees of dorsiflexion, and full range of inversion and eversion.
An X-ray was taken of the ankle at six months, which showed good tibiofibular overlap in the AP without any recurrence of the tumor.

pearls: Changes in symptoms, particularly the emergence of pain in a previously pain-free lesion and an acceleration in its growth rate, should always be viewed as an alert for the potential of malignant transformation.
Signs of secondary changes of osteochondroma should also encompass the consideration of erosion or damage to adjacent bones ​.
A thorough preoperative radiological assessment was crucial in planning the approach and keeping instrumentation ready for syndesmotic stabilization after its excision.

src.title: Extensive Osteochondroma of the Talus Presenting As Syndesmotic Joint Extension and Posterior Inferior Tibiofibular Ligament Rupture: A Reportof a Rare Case and a Review of the Literature
src.authors: Kamal Dureja, Pratheeksh P Suvarna, Amit K Sahu

complaint: A 47-year-old woman presented to the surgical oncology outpatient department with a painful, progressive swelling on the dorsum of the right foot of two months duration.

events.t: A 47-year-old woman presented to the surgical oncology outpatient department with a painful, progressive swelling on the dorsum of the right foot of two months duration.
She had no history of trauma or fever.
The patient had a 5x3 cm bony hard mass arising from the second metatarsal bone of the right foot on the dorsal aspect.
There was no evidence of popliteal or inguinal lymphadenopathy and distal motor or sensory deficits.
All distal pulses were equally felt.
She presented us with a fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) report from the soft tissue component of the metatarsal swelling, which showed features of a giant cell tumor (GCT).
The plain radiograph revealed an expansive cortical diaphyseal lesion in the right second metatarsal with punctate calcification and a periosteal reaction that was suggestive of osteosarcoma.
The chest radiograph of this patient was normal.
Due to the patient's financial constraints, an MRI of the foot could not be carried out, and we proceeded with the surgery.
A wide local excision with the right second metatarsectomy was performed (R0 en-bloc resection).
The foot was reconstructed using a 6 cm non-vascularized fibular graft using k-wire.
The postoperative period was uneventful.
On the fifth postoperative day, she was able to commence partial weight bearing, and on the 14th postoperative day, her sutures were removed.
The k-wire was removed six weeks after surgery.
The final histopathology report revealed a diagnosis of chondroblastic osteosarcoma with clear margins.

In light of the conclusive histopathology report favoring chondroblastic osteosarcoma, the patient received adjuvant chemotherapy using the MAP (high-dose methotrexate, doxorubicin, and cisplatin) protocol.
As the resection margins were tumor-free, no adjuvant radiation therapy was necessary.

pearls: Radiographically, osteosarcoma can mimic benign conditions such as aneurysmal bone cysts and chondroblastomas.
Several differential diagnoses, including benign tumors, must be considered when diagnosing and treating such patients.

The diagnosis of osteosarcoma in our case was initially challenging, as the patient presented with a swelling on the dorsum of the foot, which clinically mimicked a benign GCT, and FNAC from the soft tissue component of the swelling indicated features of a GCT.
Based on the final histopathological diagnosis of chondroblastic osteosarcoma, adjuvant chemotherapy was recommended for our patient.
It is crucial to acknowledge the limitations of our study, including the lack of MRI due to financial constraints.

src.title: Surgical Triumph Over Metatarsal Osteosarcoma: A Rare Case Report Revealing Diagnostic Challenges and Successful Management
src.authors: Sandeep Ghosh, Amar Jain, Deepak Bhojwani et al.

complaint: A 50-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, tobacco use, and coronary artery disease was referred for MALS.

events.t: A 50-year-old woman with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, tobacco use, and coronary artery disease was referred for MALS.
The patient reported a long history of postprandial abdominal pressure, nausea and vomiting, and unintentional weight loss.
Her medications included a proton pump inhibitor, cholesterol medication, and antiplatelet therapy.
Examination revealed a soft, nontender, and nondistended abdomen.
Workup for a gastrointestinal etiology was negative, including upper endoscopy, right upper quadrant ultrasound, and evaluation for inflammatory bowel disease.
Mesenteric duplex ultrasound demonstrated a CA peak systolic velocity of 522 cm/s and a SMA peak systolic velocity 135 cm/s.
Dynamic measurements were not obtained.
Computed tomography demonstrated a CMT with compression from her MAL (Fig 1), a large inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) collateral vessel, and a 1.8-cm SMA aneurysm (Fig 1).
Angiography demonstrated severe stenosis of the CA on the inspiration view and occlusion on the expiration view, with hypertrophy of the IMA and reversal of flow into the SMA (Fig 2).
After a CP block, the patient reported relief of her symptoms.

Given that her SMA aneurysm was believed to be compensatory from her CMT compression, the decision was made to proceed with MAL release without SMA aneurysm repair, because the SMA could remodel over time after the release.
A midline laparotomy was made from the xiphoid process down to the umbilicus.
The subcutaneous tissues were dissected, and the fascia was entered.
On entering the abdomen, the small bowel, large bowel, stomach, liver, and gallbladder were inspected and were unremarkable.
The gastrohepatic ligament was divided, and the patient's esophagus was retracted to the left.
The left lobe of the liver was taken down by dividing the triangular ligament and was retracted toward the patient's right underneath a fixed retractor.
The dissection was continued down to the supraceliac aorta.
The pancreas was retracted caudally, and the CMT was identified, which appeared narrowed, with post-stenotic aneurysmal dilation of the SMA.
The surrounding diaphragmatic bands were incised, with visible relief of the compression, and the nerves from the CP overlying the CMT were excised.
The abdomen was closed in standard fashion.
The patient's postoperative course was uncomplicated.
She was discharged on postoperative day 7 able to consume a general diet.
At her follow-up visit, the patient reported relief of symptoms and weight gain.
Her postoperative computed tomography scan, obtained at the 6-month follow-up, demonstrated resolved CMT compression but a persistent SMA aneurysm, which was stable in size (Fig 3).
She has remained asymptomatic postoperatively.
She provided written informed consent for the report of her case details and imaging studies.

pearls: In patients with MALS, an important collateral pathway between the CA and SMA is through the pancreaticoduodenal and dorsal pancreatic arteries, which are also the most common locations for aneurysms in MALS patients.
Current guidelines from the Society for Vascular Surgery recommend surgical repair of all SMA aneurysms regardless of size, with an endovascular approach preferred if anatomically suitable.

These guidelines also state that these patients require individualized decision-making and should be treated conservatively unless they become symptomatic or are found to have true aneurysmal degeneration.
However, we could not exclude other causes of de novo aneurysm formation and, thus, must continue regular surveillance of her SMA aneurysm.
